description: Team Topologies: team types, interaction modes, cognitive load and fracture planes for designing teams for fast flow. For an architect shaping platform and stream-aligned team boundaries.

notes.front: What does Team Topologies optimise organisations for?
notes.back: Fast flow of change: delivering value quickly, safely and sustainably by removing hand-offs and organisational friction.

notes.front: Conway's Law?
notes.back: Organisations design systems that mirror their own communication structures.
notes.analogy: Four teams building a compiler get a four-pass compiler.

notes.front: Reverse (Inverse) Conway Maneuver?
notes.back: Deliberately shape team structure and communication paths first, so the desired architecture emerges from them (e.g. one team per service).
notes.extra: Implication for architects: team boundaries are architecture decisions.

notes.front: Why is the team, not the individual, the fundamental unit of delivery?
notes.back: Modern software needs more skill and context than one person can hold; a stable team is the smallest unit that can own it end to end.

notes.front: Team-first approach?
notes.back: Optimise for the team's long-term health, purpose and cognitive load rather than individual utilisation or short-term task assignment.

notes.front: Why keep teams long-lived (years, not projects)?
notes.back: Trust, shared context and delivery speed take months to build and are reset whenever a team is reformed.
notes.extra: Bring work to stable teams rather than assembling teams around projects.

notes.front: Recommended team size in Team Topologies, and why?
notes.back: About 5–9 people (≈7). Larger teams lose deep trust and communication overhead grows.
notes.extra: Based on Dunbar's layers (~5 close, ~15 trusted, ~50, ~150); the same limits cap team-of-teams groupings.

notes.front: Team API?
notes.back: Everything other teams need to interact with a team: code and versioned interfaces, docs, communication channels and working practices.
notes.analogy: A public API for the team itself: explicit, documented, and stable enough to depend on.

notes.front: Value stream (Team Topologies sense)?
notes.back: The sequence of activities that delivers value to a customer, from idea to running software in users' hands.

notes.front: Cognitive load in Team Topologies?
notes.back: The total mental effort a team spends to do its work; it caps how much responsibility a team can own.

notes.front: Which type of cognitive load is the inherent difficulty of the task itself (e.g. domain or algorithm complexity)?
notes.back: Intrinsic cognitive load.

notes.front: Which type of cognitive load comes from the environment the work happens in (bad tooling, flaky pipelines, poor docs)?
notes.back: Extraneous cognitive load. Minimise it.
notes.analogy: Fighting a jammed printer before you can write the report.

notes.front: Which type of cognitive load goes into learning and improving the domain itself (the valuable work)?
notes.back: Germane cognitive load.

notes.text: Cognitive-load strategy: {{c1::eliminate}} extraneous load (e.g. via a platform) so teams have capacity for {{c2::germane}} load, the domain learning that adds value.

notes.front: Why size software domains to a team's cognitive load, not the reverse?
notes.back: A team owning more than it can hold in its head ships lower quality, slows down and burns out; the boundary should match what one team can reliably own.

notes.text: The four fundamental team types: {{c1::stream-aligned}}, {{c2::enabling}}, {{c3::complicated-subsystem}} and {{c4::platform}} teams.

notes.front: Stream-aligned team?
notes.back: A team aligned to one valuable stream of work (product, service, user journey, persona) that delivers to the customer end to end.

notes.front: Why is the stream-aligned team the primary team type?
notes.back: Value flows to customers through it; the other three types exist to reduce stream-aligned teams' cognitive load.

notes.front: Enabling team?
notes.back: Specialists who help stream-aligned teams close a capability gap for a limited time, by coaching, without doing the work for them.
notes.analogy: A driving instructor: success means you no longer need them.

notes.front: Enabling team: what failure mode must it avoid?
notes.back: Becoming a permanent dependency or bottleneck; its goal is to make stream-aligned teams autonomous.

notes.front: Complicated-subsystem team?
notes.back: Owns a part of the system needing deep specialist knowledge (e.g. a video codec or pricing model), so stream-aligned teams don't carry that load.

notes.front: When is forming a complicated-subsystem team justified?
notes.back: Only when the expertise is genuinely rare and hard to learn, and the load reduction outweighs the extra coordination.
notes.analogy: Hire an anaesthetist for the surgical team; don't send every nurse to anaesthesia school.

notes.front: Platform team and platform in Team Topologies?
notes.back: A platform team provides self-service APIs, tools, services and support run as a compelling internal product, so stream-aligned teams deliver autonomously with less cognitive load.
notes.analogy: An airport: airlines fly their own routes but self-serve runways, fuel and baggage systems instead of building them.

notes.front: Why is not every shared central team a "platform team"?
notes.back: The term implies a self-service, product-like offering; a team that just centralises work behind tickets creates hand-offs instead of reducing load.

notes.front: Thinnest Viable Platform (TVP)?
notes.back: The smallest platform that meets stream-aligned teams' current needs, avoiding building ahead of demand.
notes.extra: It can be just a wiki page of curated services and conventions.

notes.front: Platform grouping?
notes.back: A platform can be a group of several teams (of different types, even nested platforms) working under one shared mission, not always a single team.

notes.front: Enabling vs complicated-subsystem team: key difference?
notes.back: Enabling teams transfer expertise and then step back; complicated-subsystem teams own a specialist component long-term.

notes.front: Platform vs complicated-subsystem team: key difference?
notes.back: A platform offers broad self-service capabilities to many teams; a complicated-subsystem team owns one specialist component that is hard to build.

notes.text: The three team interaction modes: {{c1::collaboration}}, {{c2::X-as-a-Service}} and {{c3::facilitating}}.

notes.front: Collaboration interaction mode?
notes.back: Two teams work closely together for a defined period with shared responsibility. Fast discovery, but high cognitive load for both.

notes.front: When should collaboration mode be used, and why time-box it?
notes.back: For discovery or rapid learning across a boundary. Time-box it because sustained collaboration raises cognitive load and blurs ownership.

notes.front: X-as-a-Service interaction mode?
notes.back: One team consumes an API, tool or service another team provides, with minimal collaboration. Clear ownership and low load, less flexibility.
notes.analogy: Using a utility: you plug in and pay attention only when it breaks.

notes.front: Facilitating interaction mode?
notes.back: One team (usually enabling) helps another learn or adopt something new, clearing obstacles without doing the work.

notes.front: Collaboration vs facilitating: key difference?
notes.back: Collaboration: both teams do the work together and share responsibility. Facilitating: one team coaches, the other does and owns the work.

notes.front: Typical steady-state mode between a stream-aligned team and a platform team?
notes.back: X-as-a-Service: the stream-aligned team self-serves the platform.

notes.front: Typical mode between an enabling team and a stream-aligned team?
notes.back: Facilitating: build the capability, then step back.

notes.front: Why should two teams use one interaction mode with each other at a time?
notes.back: Mixed modes create unclear expectations and hidden hand-offs, defeating the point of naming the interaction explicitly.

notes.front: Why split systems between teams along fracture planes?
notes.back: Natural seams keep each team's part loosely coupled, reducing hand-offs and shared cognitive load.
notes.analogy: Splitting wood along the grain: it parts cleanly; across the grain it splinters.

notes.text: Fracture planes for splitting software between teams: business-domain {{c1::bounded context}}, {{c2::regulatory compliance}}, {{c3::change cadence}}, {{c4::risk}}, {{c5::performance isolation}}, {{c6::technology}}, {{c7::user personas}}.

notes.front: How does Team Topologies use DDD's bounded context?
notes.back: As the preferred fracture plane: a stream-aligned team owns a coherent bounded context of the business domain.

notes.front: What should trigger a change in team topology?
notes.back: Sensed friction, not a schedule: cognitive overload, slow flow, repeated hand-offs, or team structure misaligned with the value stream.
notes.extra: Sensing = continuously treating these signals as feedback on team boundaries and interactions.

notes.front: Why must team structures evolve rather than stay fixed?
notes.back: Static structures drift out of alignment with architecture and value streams, bringing back hand-offs and slow flow.

notes.front: Anti-pattern: staying in collaboration mode too long?
notes.back: Continuing to collaborate after the shared learning is done, inflating both teams' cognitive load; move to X-as-a-Service.
